provenance: Researched dossier with an explicitly reviewed identity match. Dates may follow a stated scholarly convention; source boundaries are independently attributed.
summary: Rome’s imperial government dominated the Mediterranean world; its eastern continuation survived long after the western imperial office ended.
currency: Gold aureus, silver denarius and bronze denominations in the early empire; later monetary systems changed.
rulers: Selected rulers: Augustus, 27 BCE–14 CE; Constantine I, 306–337 CE.
economy: Roads and sea routes circulated agricultural produce, people and other commodities across connected Mediterranean provinces.
military: Imperial authority rested on extensive military power; conquest joined regions around the Mediterranean under Roman rule.
contributions: Connected transport networks, urban architecture and Roman legal traditions shaped later Mediterranean and European societies.
origin: Augustus established predominant personal authority after the late Republic’s civil wars.
decline: The western emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed in 476; eastern Roman government continued from Constantinople.
periodNote: 476 CE is a conventional western endpoint. This record overlaps the Byzantine record because Byzantium was the eastern Roman continuation, not an unrelated new civilization.
